newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai soymeal up, maize steady to lower this week.
newsitem.headline: Thai soymeal up, maize steady to lower this week.

text.p: The Thai feedmill industry on Tuesday was awaiting a cabinet resolution on a possible raw materials tariff cut before placing orders for foreign soymeal and soybean, trade sources said.
One trader said he had a firm inquiry to buy 25,000 tonnes of 48-percent soymeal and 15,000 tonnes of soybean from the United States for October shipment.
"I hope the deal can be concluded later today whether or not the cabinet approves the tariff cuts for animal feed raw materials or not," the trader said.

Other traders said industry players were likely to buy more soymeal soon on the theory that the price of soymeal and soybean could rise further in light of forecasts for early frosts in U.S. soybean growing region.

The commerce ministry had proposed to cut the import duty on soymeal to 10 percent from 15 percent, to zero percent from five on soybean, to zero from three on corn and to 15 percent plus 140 baht/tonne (US$5.6) surcharge from 6 percent plus 1,400 baht/tonne surcharge on fishmeal.
The industry was hoping that the proposal would be approved at this Tuesday's cabinet meeting, which could be the last for outgoing Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa.
The price of benchmark 14.50 percent-moisture maize paid by feed producers was quoted around 4.30-4.50 baht a kg compared with 4.50-4.60 baht a kg last week.

"The supply was low but so was demand. It seemed like buyers were sidelined to wait for the second crop which will start entering the market by the end of next month," said a source form Thai Maize and Produce Traders Association.
Tight supply pushed the prices of locally-crushed soymeal from imported soybean up to 10.30-10.40 baht from 10.20 baht last week.
Fresh imported soymeal supply was not expected to be available until next month, industry and official sources said.
But supply shortages were partly alleviated by easier prices of fishmeal which could be used as a substitute for soymeal, trade sources said.
